Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CR2101 : Materials Thermodynamics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Basic thermodynamics: introduction and terminology, Review of basic physical chemistry, Equilibrium and types, Zeroth law of thermodynamics, Concepts of heat, work, internal energy, Enthalpy of processes, First law of thermodynamics, Born-Haber cycle.
Module 2: Second law of thermodynamics, Combined 1st and 2nd law, Efficiency, Statistical interpretation of entropy, Boltzmann equation, Entropy and disorder, Third law of thermodynamics.
Module 3: Auxiliary thermodynamic functions, Helmholtz free energy, Gibbs free energy, Chemical potential, Maxwell’s relations, Thermodynamic representation of processes, Gibbs-Helmholtz equation.
Module 5: Phase equilibria in single component systems, Variation of Gibbs free energy with pressure and temperature, Clausius-Clapeyron equation, P-T diagrams.
Module 6: Reaction equilibria in homogeneous gas mixtures, Effect of pressure and temperature on equilibrium constant.
Module 7: Reaction between gases and condensed phases, Oxidation of metals, equilibrium partial pressure of oxidation, Effect of temperature, Relative oxidation, Ellingham-Richardson diagrams.
Module 8: Thermodynamics of solutions, Raoult’s law, Henry’s law, Fugacity, Activity of components, Regular solutions, Gibbs-Duhem equation, Sub-regular solutions, Excess thermodynamic functions.
Module 9: Gibbs phase rule, Lever rule, Basics of free energy and composition diagrams for binary systems, Examples of eutectic, eutectoid, and peritectic systems.

Course Objective

1 .

To impart a basic understanding of various thermodynamic processes in materials systems at undergraduate level to Ceramic engineering students.
2 .

To provide fundamental understanding of thermodynamic principles that govern industrial ceramic processes, including oxidation, reduction, melting/solidification, phase transformation in materials.
3 .

To be able to apply fundamental thermodynamic principles for engineering solutions and for the development of new materials and processes.

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: Ability to apply basic thermodynamic principles to understand natural and synthetic materials processes.
CO2: Ability to understand phase stability and the influence of thermodynamic variables in single and multicomponent ceramic and metal systems.
CO3: Ability to independently solve numerical problems and case studies related to thermodynamic processes in ceramics and materials.
CO4: Ability to apply thermodynamic principles to carry out independent research for the development of new ceramics, alloys, materials, and composites.

Supplementary Reading

David V Ragone, Thermodynamics of Materials: Volume I and II, MIT Series in Materials Science and Engineering

2 .

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : LS3075 : Life Science Laboratory - V { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

The course includes a series of 8–10 experiments designed to provide students with hands-on experience in genetic analysis, molecular techniques, and bioinformatics tools. The experiments aim to enhance understanding of the expression, characterization, and analysis of genetic material and related processes.
Module I: Introduction to Key Model Organisms
Introduction to model organisms used in genetics research (Drosophila melanogaster, Arabidopsis thaliana, and Mus musculus). Observation of life cycles, key phenotypic traits, and handling techniques for these organisms in the laboratory. Basic techniques for maintenance and care (e.g., setting up Drosophila crosses, Arabidopsis growth, and ethical considerations in mouse handling).
Module II: Extraction and Quantification of Genomic DNA
Isolation of genomic DNA from plant or animal tissues (model organism tissue) using standard protocols. Quantification of DNA using UV-visible spectroscopy and integrity assessment through agarose gel electrophoresis.
Module III: Bioinformatics Tools for Gene Cloning
Hands-on training with SnapGene or equivalent software for designing primers and simulating cloning strategies. Planning the cloning of a target gene into an expression vector, considering restriction sites, ligation strategies, and insert orientation. Validation of the designed cloning strategy through in silico simulations.
Module IV: Amplification of Target DNA Using Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
Amplification of a specific gene using PCR. Optimization of PCR conditions and visualization of amplified products through agarose gel electrophoresis.
Module V: Restriction Digestion and Ligation in an Expression Vector
Digestion of plasmid DNA using specific restriction enzymes. Visualization of restriction patterns using gel electrophoresis and estimation of fragment sizes. Ligation into the desired vector and confirmation of cloning.
Module VI: Cytogenetics and Chromosome Analysis
Preparation of mitotic or meiotic spreads from plant or animal samples. Observation of chromosomal structures, ploidy, and abnormalities using light microscopy. Hands-on training for karyotyping using software (e.g., KaryoMeasure).
Module VII: Inducing Mutations and Identifying Phenotypic Changes
Induction of mutations in Drosophila or microbial systems using chemical or physical mutagens (e.g., EMS or UV radiation). Screening for altered phenotypes such as morphological changes, loss of function, or resistance traits.
Module VIII: Pedigree Analysis
Interpretation of pedigree charts for autosomal dominant/recessive, X-linked, and mitochondrial inheritance. Determination of carrier status, prediction of inheritance risks, and discussion of real-world applications in genetic counseling.
Module IX: CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing Simulation
Designing CRISPR guide RNAs for targeted genome editing. Simulation of gene knockout or modification using in silico tools and interpretation of outcomes.

Course Objective

1 .

Develop Practical Skills in Genetic Analysis:
Equip students with hands-on experience in key genetic techniques, including DNA extraction, PCR amplification, cloning, and mutagenesis, to analyze and manipulate genetic material effectively.
2 .

Integrate Bioinformatics and Laboratory Techniques:
Enable students to utilize bioinformatics tools for gene cloning, sequence analysis, and genome editing simulations, bridging computational and experimental approaches in modern genetics.
3 .

Understand Model Organisms and Inheritance Patterns:
Familiarize students with the use of model organisms (Drosophila melanogaster, Arabidopsis thaliana, Mus musculus) for genetic research and the principles of Mendelian and non-Mendelian inheritance through practical experiments and analysis.

Course Outcome

1 .

By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Perform essential genetic experiments, including DNA extraction, PCR, cloning, mutagenesis, and cytogenetic analysis, with proficiency in laboratory techniques and tools.
2. Utilize bioinformatics software for designing primers, planning gene cloning strategies, and simulating genome editing processes to complement experimental approaches.
3. Analyze Genetic Material and Phenotypes: Interpret results from molecular and cytogenetic experiments, including DNA quantification, chromosome analysis, and phenotypic screening of mutations.
4. Work with Model Organisms: Demonstrate knowledge of handling and maintaining model organisms (Drosophila melanogaster, Arabidopsis thaliana, and Mus musculus) and their relevance in genetic studies.
5. Evaluate Genetic Inheritance Patterns: Analyze pedigree charts and genetic data to predict inheritance risks and understand the principles of Mendelian and non-Mendelian genetics in real-world contexts.

Supplementary Reading
